Stepanov2 1 Saint-Petersburg University 2 Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute, Saint-Petersburg, Russia maria-shukht@yandex.ru An empirical model of subrelativistic (40-275 keV) electron (SE) fluxes at the geostationary orbit is proposed. The model suggests that the main factor, driving the SE fluxes, is injections, which are superimposed on existing background. GOES-13 and GOES-15 observations in 2017 are used for the model, which is further tested on data from 2012-2016. Results for both spacecraft, separated by 4 hours in MLT, are similar. The background fluxes demonstrate alike MLT variation, depending on electron energy. The effect of injections is described by linear filters, with the positive MPB index [1] increment as the input. The model reproduces the main observational features of SE fluxes: midnight-dawn maximum, evening minimum and energy dispersion, confirming the drift mechanism as the basic governing factor. Comparison with observations gives rather good correlations (~0.7) for lower energy channels (50 and 75 keV), whereas for higher energies the correlations decrease. It confirms that just the fluxes with energies below 100-200 keV are really injected. The best correlations are manifested for moderate geomagnetic activity, and even supersubstorms demonstrate reasonable results, some of them manifesting the Kennel-Petschek saturation. content_preview: GC2026-STP050 Variations in the F2-layer critical frequency: dependence on the choice of solar activity index Sargylana E. Kobyakova1 , Artem Y. Gololobov1 , Rustam R. Karimov1 , Alexandr E. Stepanov1 1 Y.G. Shafer Institute of Cosmophysical Research and Aeronomy of the Siberian Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences karimovrim@gmail.com Variations in the F2-layer critical frequency (foF2) as a function of the solar activity index choice were studied using annual mean foF2 values from the Yakutsk ionospheric station (62.01° N, 129.43° E) over the period 1957–2017. It is shown that both the magnitude and sign of the foF2 trend at subauroral latitudes are significantly influenced by the choice of solar activity index. Trends derived from six different solar activity indices—F10.7, F30, Mg II, He II, SSN, and Lyman‑α—were compared. The F30 and Mg II indices demonstrated the best performance, followed by F10.7 and Lyman‑α, while the SSN and He II indices proved to be less suitable for trend analysis. The results indicate that the negative trends obtained with F30 and Mg II are approximately two to three times larger in magnitude than those derived from F10.7 and Lyman‑α. Therefore, for studies of long-term ionospheric variability in the subauroral region based on data from the Yakutsk station and employing annual mean values, the F30 index is recommended as the most appropriate solar proxy. The second integral characteristic is the local magnetic constant, whose value does not depend on the orientation of the equivalent dipole [1]. The equivalent magnetic dipole is understood as a dipole located near the center of the Earth and producing the magnetic field observed at a given point. The equivalent dipole is characterized by the magnitude of its magnetic moment, the distance from the dipole center to the observation point, and its orientation relative to the Earth's rotation axis [2, 3]. The advantage of analyzing the behavior of these integral parameters, as compared with analyzing individual elements of the geomagnetic field, lies in the transition from a more complex and sometimes contradictory triple dependence of the measured elements to a simpler double dependence of the integral characteristics. content_preview: GC2026-PERM034 The simplest model of the geodynamo Sergey Starchenko1 1 Pushkov Institute of Terrestrial Magnetism, Ionosphere and Radiowave Propagation of the Russian Academy of Sciences sstarchenko@mail.ru We integrate the scalar product of the induction equation and the magnetic field vector over the entire dynamo volume. We obtain an evolution equation for the magnetic energy supported by the integral power of the Lorentz magnetic force and counteracted by the integral power of magnetic diffusion. Approximating the corresponding integrals through the mean square magnetic field and a given Lorentz force power, we obtain a linear and inhomogeneous ordinary differential equation for the square of the field. For a given power constant over time and any initial condition (except zero), the solution stabilizes at a value dependent on the dynamo parameters. Moreover, the smaller the initial field, the larger the time derivative of the field, up to explosive growth. For the geodynamo, the aforementioned parameters are approximately determined from observations, resulting in a total magnetic energy of 30 ZJ and a field of 100 G, which are consistent with existing studies. If we specify the power as the sum of a constant and a harmonic function of time, then we can roughly model the observed dynamics of the geomagnetic field.

Schmidt Institute of Physics of the Earth, Russian Academy of Sciences goev@idg.ras.ru Mantle transition zone (MTZ), occurring at depths of approximately 410 and 660 km, is the region where olivine transforms into its denser states upon reaching specific P-T conditions. Accordingly, the boundaries at which these transitions occur are characterized by a sharp increase in seismic velocities. It has been established that when these boundaries interact with a cold slab (for example, in the Kuril-Kamchatka zone), their depths can vary significantly. One of the most effective tools for studying the local characteristics of these boundaries is the analysis of Ps converted waves (the PRF method). However, to achieve reliable results, it is necessary to analyze long-term records of broadband seismic data. For this reason, detailed studies of the depths of these boundaries in the Russian Far East zone were practically absent. In recent decades, the seismic networks of the Kamchatka and Sakhalin branches of the GS RAS have developed significantly, and now it compose more than 50 broadband seismometers. Processing of this data has, for the first time, made it possible to estimate the local relief of the 410 and 660 km discontinuities in the Russian Far East zone. content_preview: GC2026-SGG049 Geomechanical effects of cyclic impact on the bottomhole formation zone in laboratory conditions Zakhar Ivanov1 1 Perm National Research Polytechnic University zakhar.ivanov.2013@gmail.com The bottomhole formation zone (BFZ) is a key element of the "reservoir – well" system, determining the productivity of producing wells. During operation, the filtration characteristics of the BFZ deteriorate due to colmatation and mechanical deformations. Traditional treatment methods are often expensive and not always effective, especially in poorly consolidated reservoirs. Cyclic impact is considered a promising method for controlling filtration processes, based on creating alternating pressure gradients by periodically opening and closing the well. The geomechanical essence of the method lies in the fact that a sharp drawdown creates high pressure gradients, causing elastic deformations of the porous matrix and the destruction of colmatating deposits. Subsequent well shut-in leads to stress relaxation and redistribution of solid particles. Repeated cycles result in the accumulation of irreversible deformations, changes in grain packing, and transformation of the BFZ filtration structure. To experimentally study the geomechanical effects, a laboratory setup was developed featuring a granular reservoir model and a controlled outlet valve that automatically opens and closes at a specified frequency. During the experiments, pressure drops across sections of the model and fluid flow rate were recorded to calculate permeability changes as an indicator of deformation processes.
